questions.title: Which of the following is considered a primary lymphoid organ?
questions.question: Which of the following is considered a primary lymphoid organ?

explanations.A: Correct. Bone marrow is a primary (central) lymphoid organ, along with the thymus — together these are the sites where B and T lymphocytes develop and mature before ever meeting antigen. This is what distinguishes a primary lymphoid organ from a secondary one: primary organs generate and mature naive lymphocytes, while secondary organs (lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, MALT) are where those already-mature lymphocytes encounter antigen and mount a response. Bone marrow additionally performs haematopoiesis, generating every blood cell lineage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymph nodes are a secondary lymphoid organ — a site where mature lymphocytes are activated by antigen, not where they develop.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ that filters blood and initiates responses to blood-borne antigen, not a site of lymphocyte development.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tonsils are secondary lymphoid (mucosa-associated) tissue that samples antigen at the pharynx, not a primary developmental organ.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: Identify bone marrow as a primary lymphoid organ, distinguishing it from the secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils).

questions.title: Which of the following statements isn't true about lymph nodes?
questions.question: Which of the following statements isn't true about lymph nodes?

options.B: Site of initiation of immune response
options.C: Act as immunological filter of tissues
options.D: Site of maturation of B cells
options.E: Harbor large number of APCs, B & T cells

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS true) — lymph nodes do trap microbes and antigen draining in from the tissues they serve, which is exactly why this is not the exception the question asks for.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS true) — lymph nodes are where naive lymphocytes first encounter antigen and where an immune response is initiated.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS true) — lymph nodes filter lymph draining from tissues, removing and presenting antigen much as the spleen filters blood.
explanations.D: Correct. Site of maturation of B cells is the false statement, and therefore the answer. B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow, a primary lymphoid organ; only afterwards do mature, naive B cells traffic to lymph nodes to be activated by antigen. Everything else listed — trapping antigen, filtering lymph, initiating responses, and housing large numbers of APCs, B cells and T cells — genuinely describes lymph-node function.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this IS true) — lymph nodes house dense populations of APCs, B cells and T cells, which is what makes them the site of immune-response initiation.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: Identify B-cell maturation as a bone-marrow, not a lymph-node, function.

questions.title: Removal of thymus affects the function of:
questions.question: Removal of thymus affects the function of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow, independent of the thymus, so thymectomy does not impair B-cell function.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) are innate myeloid cells that do not depend on thymic maturation.
explanations.C: Correct. The thymus is the primary lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes complete their maturation and selection. Removing the thymus removes this maturation site, so T-lymphocyte generation and function are selectively impaired. B lymphocytes, granulocytes, monocytes and NK cells all mature or develop independently of the thymus and are therefore unaffected by thymectomy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Monocytes are innate myeloid cells derived from bone-marrow progenitors and do not require thymic maturation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. NK cells are innate lymphoid cells that mature largely independent of the thymus, unlike T cells.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: State that thymus removal selectively impairs T-lymphocyte function, since the thymus is the T-cell maturation site.

questions.title: Which type of cells is increased in acute infections of bacterial origin?
questions.question: Which type of cells is increased in acute infections of bacterial origin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Basophils are not characteristically raised in acute bacterial infection; they are more associated with allergic and parasitic responses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Eosinophils rise in parasitic infection and allergic disease, not acute bacterial infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymphocytosis is the characteristic response to viral, not acute bacterial, infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. NK cells are not the leukocyte population that characteristically rises with acute bacterial infection.
explanations.E: Correct. Acute infections of bacterial origin characteristically drive a rise in circulating neutrophils (neutrophilia), reflecting the neutrophil's role as the first-responder phagocyte recruited to clear extracellular bacteria. This contrasts with the lymphocytosis seen in viral infection and the eosinophilia of parasitic or allergic disease, making the leukocyte differential a useful clinical clue to the type of infection present.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: State that neutrophils are the leukocyte that characteristically rises in acute bacterial infection.

questions.title: The largest lymphoid organ that clears particulate matter from blood & concentrates blood-borne pathogens is the:
questions.question: The largest lymphoid organ that clears particulate matter from blood & concentrates blood-borne pathogens is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peyer's patches are gut-associated lymphoid tissue sampling intestinal antigen, not the largest lymphoid organ and not a blood filter.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tonsils sample antigen at the pharynx; they are not the largest lymphoid organ and do not filter blood.
explanations.C: Correct. The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ in the body and is specialised to filter blood rather than lymph — this is the key distinction from lymph nodes, which filter lymph. By concentrating and clearing particulate matter and blood-borne pathogens as blood passes through it, the spleen mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigen and also removes aged or damaged red cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ (T-cell maturation site), not the blood-filtering organ described here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bone marrow is a primary lymphoid organ (haematopoiesis and B-cell maturation), not the largest lymphoid organ and not the blood filter described here.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: Identify the spleen as the largest lymphoid organ and the organ that filters blood (as opposed to lymph nodes, which filter lymph).

questions.title: Which type of cells is increased in viral infection?
questions.question: Which type of cells is increased in viral infection?

explanations.A: Correct. Viral infections characteristically drive a rise in circulating lymphocytes (lymphocytosis), reflecting expansion of the antiviral T- and NK-cell response as the body mounts cell-mediated defences against infected host cells. This is a useful clinical differentiator from acute bacterial infection, which instead drives neutrophilia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neutrophilia is the characteristic response to acute bacterial, not viral, infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eosinophils rise in parasitic infection and allergic disease, not viral infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Basophils are not the leukocyte population characteristically raised in viral infection.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: State that lymphocytes are the leukocyte that characteristically rises in viral infection.

questions.title: Which of the following cells are notable for their presence at the site of helminth infection?
questions.question: Which of the following cells are notable for their presence at the site of helminth infection?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Basophils contribute to allergic-type responses but are not the marker cell most notable at helminth infection sites.
explanations.B: Correct. Eosinophils are the myeloid leukocyte that characteristically rises in allergy and parasitic (especially helminth) infection, and are notably recruited to and found at the site of helminth infection. There, they degranulate and release toxic granule contents directly onto the parasite's surface, since helminths are far too large for a single cell to phagocytose. This extracellular, granule-mediated killing is the eosinophil's signature role and the reason it is the marker cell of parasitic and allergic disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymphocytes are not the cell type notably concentrated at helminth infection sites; they are more associated with viral infection responses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Monocytes are general-purpose phagocytes, not the cell notably marking helminth infection.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Neutrophils are the marker of acute bacterial, not helminth, infection.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: Identify eosinophils as the cell type notable at the site of helminth infection.

questions.title: A monocyte may leave the blood & differentiate into:
questions.question: A monocyte may leave the blood & differentiate into:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mast cells develop from a distinct myeloid progenitor lineage, not from circulating monocytes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Platelets are anucleate cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes, not from monocyte differentiation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymphocytes are a separate lineage entirely (derived from lymphoid, not monocytic, progenitors).
explanations.D: Correct. A monocyte that migrates out of the blood into tissue differentiates into a macrophage (or, in some tissues, a dendritic cell). This tissue macrophage then carries out phagocytosis, antigen presentation and cytokine secretion at the local site.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: State that a monocyte leaving the blood and entering tissue differentiates into a macrophage.

questions.title: Dendritic cells are involved in:
questions.question: Dendritic cells are involved in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Suppressing the immune system is a regulatory T-cell function, not the defining role of dendritic cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Destroying target cells describes cytotoxic T cells or NK cells, not the dendritic cell's role.
explanations.C: Correct. Dendritic cells are the professional antigen-presenting cell best suited to activate naive T lymphocytes. They capture antigen in peripheral tissue, process it, and migrate to secondary lymphoid organs, where they display peptide fragments on MHC molecules to T cells. This is what initiates the adaptive T-cell response, making dendritic cells the essential bridge between innate antigen capture and adaptive T-cell activation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Complement activation is carried out by the complement protein cascade, not by dendritic cells themselves.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: State that dendritic cells present antigen to T cells, activating naive T lymphocytes.

questions.title: A cell utilizing lysosomal enzymes to kill pathogens is:
questions.question: A cell utilizing lysosomal enzymes to kill pathogens is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. NK cells kill their targets by releasing perforin and granzymes, not lysosomal enzymes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells (Tc) also kill via perforin and granzyme release, a different mechanism from lysosomal-enzyme killing.
explanations.C: Correct. After phagocytosing a pathogen, the neutrophil's principal killing mechanism is degranulation of lysosomal (azurophilic and specific granule) enzymes into the phagosome, working alongside the oxidative burst to destroy the ingested organism. This distinguishes phagocyte killing of ingested extracellular pathogens from the perforin/granzyme killing NK and cytotoxic T cells use against infected or tumour host cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Helper T cells (Th) coordinate the immune response via cytokines and costimulation; they do not themselves kill pathogens using lysosomal enzymes.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: Identify the neutrophil as the cell that uses lysosomal enzymes to kill ingested pathogens, distinguishing this from perforin/granzyme killing.

questions.title: The role of primary lymphoid organs in the immune system:
questions.question: The role of primary lymphoid organs in the immune system:

options.A: Expose T cells to foreign antigens
options.B: Primary site for Ab synthesis & release
options.C: Filter blood & trap blood borne antigens
options.D: Provide an environment for maturation of B & T cells
options.E: Line mucosal surfaces of the body for efficient Ag contact

explanations.A: Incorrect. Exposing T cells to foreign antigen is a secondary-lymphoid-organ role (lymph nodes, spleen), not a primary-organ one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Antibody synthesis and release happens in secondary lymphoid organs, where activated plasma cells reside, not in the primary organs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Filtering blood and trapping blood-borne antigen describes the spleen, a secondary lymphoid organ.
explanations.D: Correct. Bone marrow and thymus are primary lymphoid organs and are identified as the sites of B- and T-cell development and maturation — providing the environment in which lymphocytes complete this process before ever meeting antigen. This developmental role is what distinguishes primary lymphoid organs from secondary ones, which instead activate already-mature lymphocytes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lining mucosal surfaces for antigen contact describes mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), a secondary lymphoid tissue.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: State that primary lymphoid organs provide the environment for B- and T-cell maturation, distinguishing this from secondary-organ roles.

questions.title: Haematopoietic stem cells are pluripotent, in that:
questions.question: Haematopoietic stem cells are pluripotent, in that:

options.B: They are T & B cells of different specificities
options.C: They can develop into any blood cell
options.D: They produce cells of a single lineage

explanations.A: Incorrect. Antigen specificity is a property of mature T and B lymphocyte receptors, not of haematopoietic stem cells, which have no antigen receptor at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Haematopoietic stem cells are not themselves T and B cells; T and B lymphocytes are just two of the many lineages a stem cell can ultimately give rise to.
explanations.C: Correct. Haematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow are pluripotent. A single stem cell can give rise to any blood cell lineage, both myeloid (granulocytes, monocytes, red cells, platelets) and lymphoid (T cells, B cells, NK cells), rather than being restricted to one lineage. This is a property of the progenitor cell itself, quite separate from the antigen specificity that mature T- and B-cell receptors later acquire.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Producing cells of a single lineage describes a unipotent progenitor, not a pluripotent stem cell — pluripotency means the opposite, the ability to give rise to multiple/any lineage.

questions.topic: Organs and cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: State that haematopoietic stem cell pluripotency means the ability to develop into any blood cell lineage.
